## V Angular-Momentum Transport View of Radial Currents

Interestingly, comparing the expression $-E/rB$ evaluated by MITNS, as shown in figure 3, to the angular velocity profile in figure 1 shows there are some differences between them, when solving the system of equations for a small but finite $\tilde{\rho}_{i0}$ . The $\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}$ azimuthal drift discussed in Kolmes et al. [30] is recovered in the limit of $\tilde{\rho}_{i0}\rightarrow 0$ .

For the $\tilde{\rho}_{i0}=0.01$ case, the most visible features in figure 3, are the non-zero derivative at $r=0$ , and the non-monotonicity of the green curve, even though the angular velocity profile is monotonous in figure 1. This means that the solution to equation (15) contains information about the diamagnetic drift as well as $-E/rB$ .

For the $\tilde{\rho}_{i0}=0.1$ case, the diamagnetic drift $p^{\prime}/neB$ , which was assumed to be $\sim\mathcal{O}(\delta E/B)$ , becomes leading-order, as the pressure varies across a much smaller domain. The diamagnetic angular frequency,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{p^{\prime}}{rneB}=\frac{T_{0}}{R^{2}eB_{0}}\frac{\tilde{p}^{\prime}}{\tilde{r}\tilde{n}\tilde{B}}=\frac{v_{thi}}{R}\tilde{\rho}_{i0}\frac{\tilde{p}^{\prime}}{\tilde{r}\tilde{n}\tilde{B}}, $$

with the dimensionless $\tilde{p}^{\prime}/\tilde{r}\tilde{n}\tilde{B}$ (plotted in Figure 4), is $\sim\mathcal{O}(3)$ . In order to make it an order smaller than $\tilde{\omega}$ (lower-left panel in Figure 1), a $\tilde{\rho}_{i0}\ll 0.12/3\sim 0.04$ is required.

In this section, we aim to expand upon the ordering of the equations of motion for N-fluids, derive the angular velocity and density profiles in terms of the cross-field particle fluxes, and show the solution presented in III is a particular solution obtained for a specific ordering of the particle flux magnitude. The small parameters in the expansion presented in this section are formally constants, rather than a function of the solution, which is easier to handle. Additionally, we explicitly keep the inner boundary terms such as in equation (30), (38) and (39), which are set to zero in Kolmes et al. [30] equation (48), for example. These boundary terms would be useful in annular geometries used for homopolar generators or some mass filter applications.

Writing the equations of motion in term of angular momentum, rather than linear momentum, casts the viscous torque term in a diffusion form. This form enables the angular momentum equation to be written in a finite-volume form, which is computationally conservative scheme.

The continuity equation, and the radial particle flux,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial n_{s}}{\partial t}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Gamma_{s}=s_{s}, \displaystyle\Gamma_{s}=rn_{s}v_{sr}=\Gamma_{s}(r_{i})+\int_{r_{i}}^{r}\left(s_{s}-\frac{\partial n_{s}}{\partial t}\right)r^{\prime}dr^{\prime}~, $$

are the driving mechanisms for the system dynamics, and they are a reasonable boundary condition to experimentally impose.

The angular momentum conservation equation,

$$ \displaystyle\ell_{s}\doteq rm_{s}n_{s}v_{s\theta}=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{P}_{s}\cdot\hat{z}, $$

$$ \frac{\partial\ell_{s}}{\partial t}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\frac{\ell_{s}\Gamma_{s}}{n_{s}}+Z_{s}e\Gamma_{s}B_{z}=\sum_{s^{\prime}}\left(\nu_{s^{\prime}s}\ell_{s^{\prime}}-\nu_{ss^{\prime}}\ell_{s}\right)\\
+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}r^{3}\left[\eta_{s1}\omega_{s}^{\prime}-\eta_{s3}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\frac{\Gamma_{s}}{r^{2}n_{s}}\right)\right]+r\sum_{s^{\prime}}f_{ss^{\prime}\theta}+\ell_{s}^{src},~ $$

is written here as an advection-diffusion equation for each species, with source terms corresponding to the Lorentz torque on the left hand side, and the friction and Nernst torques on the right hand side. The last term, $\ell^{src}_{s}$ indicates other sources of angular momentum, such as the injection of particles with non-zero angular velocity. In that case, $\ell^{src}_{s}=r^{2}m_{s}s_{s}\omega_{s}^{src}$ . We shall take this term to be zero from now.

The radial component of the momentum equation, for $P_{sr}\doteq m_{s}n_{s}v_{sr}$ ,

$$ \frac{\partial P_{sr}}{\partial t}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}rP_{sr}v_{sr}+p_{s}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{r}\ell_{s}\omega_{s}+Z_{s}en_{s}\left(E_{r}+r\omega_{s}B_{z}\right)\\
+\sum_{s^{\prime}}\left(\nu_{s^{\prime}s}P_{s^{\prime}r}-\nu_{ss^{\prime}}P_{sr}\right)\\
+\frac{1}{r^{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}r^{3}\left[\eta_{s1}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\frac{v_{sr}}{r}\right)+\eta_{s3}\omega_{s}^{\prime}\right]+P_{sr}^{src}, $$

can be written in a form such that the viscosity is a diffusion term. This allows for a conservative-form solution, as already discussed.

Using

$$ \displaystyle M_{s}\doteq rm_{s}n_{s}v_{sr}=\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{P}_{s}=m_{s}\Gamma_{s}, $$

the conservation equation for $M_{s}$ is

$$ \frac{\partial M_{s}}{\partial t}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\frac{M_{s}\Gamma_{s}}{n_{s}}+r^{2}p_{s}\right)=2p_{s}+\frac{M_{s}\Gamma_{s}}{r^{2}n_{s}}+\omega_{s}\ell_{s}\\
+Z_{s}en_{s}r\left(E_{r}+r\omega_{s}B_{z}\right)+\sum_{s^{\prime}}\left(\nu_{s^{\prime}s}M_{s^{\prime}}-\nu_{ss^{\prime}}M_{s}\right)\\
+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}r^{3}\left[\eta_{s1}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\frac{v_{sr}}{r}\right)+\eta_{s3}\omega_{s}^{\prime}\right]+M_{s}^{src}. $$

In steady state, the integral from of the two equations, (35), (32):

$$ \frac{\ell_{s}\Gamma_{s}}{n_{s}}\Big|_{r_{i}}^{r}+Z_{s}e\int_{r_{i}}^{r}\Gamma_{s}B_{z}r^{\prime}dr^{\prime}=\\
\sum_{s^{\prime}}\int_{r_{i}}^{r}\left(\nu_{s^{\prime}s}\ell_{s^{\prime}}-\nu_{ss^{\prime}}\ell_{s}+f_{ss^{\prime}\theta}r^{\prime}\right)r^{\prime}dr^{\prime}\\
+r^{3}\left[\eta_{s1}\omega_{s}^{\prime}-\eta_{s3}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\frac{\Gamma_{s}}{r^{2}n_{s}}\right)\right]_{r_{i}}^{r}, $$

$$ \left[\frac{M_{s}\Gamma_{s}}{n_{s}}+r^{2}p_{s}\right]_{r_{i}}^{r}=\int_{r_{i}}^{r}\left(2p_{s}+\frac{M_{s}\Gamma_{s}}{r^{\prime 2}n_{s}}+\omega_{s}\ell_{s}\right)r^{\prime}dr^{\prime}\\
+Z_{s}e\int_{r_{i}}^{r}n_{s}\left(E_{r}+r^{\prime}\omega_{s}B_{z}\right)r^{\prime 2}dr^{\prime}\\
+\sum_{s^{\prime}}\int_{r_{i}}^{r}\left(\nu_{s^{\prime}s}M_{s^{\prime}}-\nu_{ss^{\prime}}M_{s}\right)r^{\prime}dr^{\prime}\\
+r^{3}\left[\eta_{s1}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\frac{\Gamma_{s}}{r^{2}n_{s}}\right)+\eta_{s3}\omega_{s}^{\prime}\right]_{r_{i}}^{r}, $$

where integrals of the form $\int_{r_{i}}^{r}\cdot\ r^{\prime}dr^{\prime}$ should de understood as volume average in the annular volume bounded by $r_{i}$ and $r$ .

Summing over all species, the friction forces cancel, and the electric field term drops off due to quasi-neutrality.

$$ \sum_{s}m_{s}r^{2}\omega_{s}\Gamma_{s}\Big|_{r_{i}}^{r}+\int_{r_{i}}^{r}CB_{z}r^{\prime}dr^{\prime}=\\
\sum_{s}r^{3}\left[\eta_{s1}\omega_{s}^{\prime}-\eta_{s3}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\frac{\Gamma_{s}}{r^{2}n_{s}}\right)\right]_{r_{i}}^{r}, $$

$$ \sum_{s}\left[m_{s}\frac{\Gamma_{s}^{2}}{n_{s}}+r^{2}p_{s}\right]_{r_{i}}^{r}=\sum_{s}Z_{s}e\int_{r_{i}}^{r}n_{s}\omega_{s}B_{z}r^{\prime 3}dr^{\prime}\\
+\sum_{s}\int_{r_{i}}^{r}\left(2p_{s}+m_{s}\frac{\Gamma_{s}^{2}}{r^{\prime 2}n_{s}}+\omega_{s}\ell_{s}\right)r^{\prime}dr^{\prime}\\
+\sum_{s}r^{3}\left[\eta_{s1}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\frac{\Gamma_{s}}{r^{2}n_{s}}\right)+\eta_{s3}\omega_{s}^{\prime}\right]_{r_{i}}^{r}. $$

These equations do not depend on the electric field, and we will show their equivalence to equations (15) and (16). The leading order $\omega$ , even though it must be of $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{E}{rB}\right)$ , by the choice of the Braginskii transport coefficients, may contain information from other particle drifts.

### V.1 Nondimensionalization

Nondimensionalizing the equations of motion would factor out small parameters that would be used in an asymptotic expansion.

Denoting $X=X_{0}\tilde{X}$ , with $X_{0}$ being a reference quantity;

$$ \displaystyle m_{0}=m_{p}, \displaystyle v_{0}=\sqrt{T_{0}/m_{p}}, \displaystyle r_{0}=R, \displaystyle\Gamma_{0}=Rn_{0}v_{0}, \displaystyle C_{0}=eRn_{0}v_{0}, \displaystyle\eta_{30}=\frac{n_{0}T_{0}}{\Omega_{p0}}, \displaystyle\eta_{10}=\frac{n_{0}T_{0}\nu_{0}}{\Omega_{p0}^{2}}, \displaystyle R_{ss^{\prime}0}=m_{0}n_{0}\nu_{0}v_{0}, \displaystyle f_{ss^{\prime}0}=\frac{n_{0}\nu_{0}T_{0}}{\Omega_{p0}R}=m_{0}n_{0}\nu_{0}v_{0}\tilde{\rho}_{p0} $$

with $R$ being the outer domain radius.

The dimensionless equations feature the two small parameters $\tilde{\rho}_{p0}=v_{0}/\Omega_{p0}R$ , and $\epsilon=\nu_{0}/\Omega_{p0}$ . They are ordered such that $1\gg\epsilon\gg\tilde{\rho}_{p0}$ .

The steady-state dimensionless angular momentum for a single fluid species is,

$$ \tilde{m}_{s}\tilde{r}^{2}\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}\tilde{\omega}_{s}\Big|_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}+\frac{1}{\tilde{\rho}_{p0}}\int_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}Z_{s}\tilde{r}^{\prime}\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}\tilde{B}_{z}d\tilde{r}^{\prime}=\\
\tilde{\rho}_{p0}\tilde{r}^{3}\left[\epsilon\tilde{\eta}_{s1}\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{\prime}-\tilde{\eta}_{s3}\frac{\partial}{\partial\tilde{r}}\left(\frac{\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}}{\tilde{r}^{2}\tilde{n}_{s}}\right)\right]\Bigg|_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}\\
+\epsilon\int_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}\sum_{s^{\prime}}\left(\frac{1}{\tilde{\rho}_{p0}}\tilde{R}_{ss^{\prime}\theta}+\tilde{f}_{ss^{\prime}\theta}\right)\tilde{r}^{\prime 2}d\tilde{r}^{\prime}. $$

The equation for the entire plasma is,

$$ \sum_{s}\tilde{r}^{2}\tilde{m}_{s}\Gamma_{s}\tilde{\omega}_{s}\Big|_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}=\tilde{\rho}_{p0}\epsilon\tilde{r}^{3}\sum_{s}\tilde{\eta}_{s1}\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{\prime}\Big|_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}\\
-\tilde{\rho}_{p0}\tilde{r}^{3}\sum_{s}\tilde{\eta}_{s3}\frac{\partial}{\partial\tilde{r}}\left(\frac{\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}}{\tilde{r}^{2}\tilde{n}_{s}}\right)\Bigg|_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}-\frac{1}{\tilde{\rho}_{p0}}\int_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}\tilde{r}^{\prime}\tilde{C}\tilde{B}_{z}d\tilde{r}^{\prime}. $$

We shall order the angular velocity and source terms in the two small parameters using $\tilde{X}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\tilde{\rho}_{p0}^{\alpha}\epsilon^{\beta}\tilde{X}^{(\alpha,\beta)}$ , and restrict $\tilde{\omega}_{s}$ such that its leading term is $\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{(0,0)}$ .

Equation (49), when expanded to $\mathcal{O}(\tilde{\rho}_{p0}^{k})$ , $k=-1,0$ yield,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}Z_{s}\tilde{r}^{\prime}\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}^{(k+1,0)}\tilde{B}_{z}d\tilde{r}^{\prime}=0, \displaystyle\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}^{(0,0)}=\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}^{(1,0)}=0. $$

To $\mathcal{O}(\tilde{\rho}_{p0}^{-1}\epsilon)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle Z_{s}\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}^{(0,1)}\tilde{B}_{z}=\sum_{s^{\prime}}\left(\tilde{m}_{s}\tilde{n}_{s}\tilde{\nu}_{ss^{\prime}}\tilde{r}(\tilde{\omega}_{s^{\prime}}^{(0,0)}-\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{(0,0)})+\tilde{f}_{ss^{\prime}\theta}^{(-1,0)}\right)\tilde{r}. $$

Here, $\tilde{f}_{ss^{\prime}\theta}^{(-1,0)}$ is understood as the dimensionless (4) with dimensionless temperature gradients of $\mathcal{O}(\tilde{\rho}_{p0}^{-1})$ .

To $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$ :

$$ \int_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}\sum_{s^{\prime}}\left(\tilde{r}\tilde{m}_{s}\tilde{n}_{s}\tilde{\nu}_{ss^{\prime}}(\tilde{\omega}_{s^{\prime}}^{(1,0)}-\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{(1,0)})+\tilde{f}_{ss^{\prime}\theta}^{(0,0)}\right)\tilde{r}^{\prime 2}d\tilde{r}^{\prime}\\

$$ \sum_{s}\tilde{m}_{s}\left[\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}^{(1,1)}\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{(1,0)}\right]_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}+\tilde{r}\sum_{s}\tilde{\eta}_{s3}\frac{\partial}{\partial\tilde{r}}\left(\frac{\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}^{(1,1)}}{\tilde{r}^{2}\tilde{n}_{s}}\right)\Bigg|_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}=\\

$$ \left[\tilde{m}_{s}\frac{\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}^{2}}{\tilde{n}_{s}}+\tilde{r}^{2}\tilde{p}_{s}\right]_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}=\frac{1}{\tilde{\rho}_{p0}}Z_{s}\int_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}\tilde{n}_{s}\left[\tilde{E}_{r}+\tilde{r}^{\prime}\tilde{\omega}_{s}\tilde{B}_{z}\right]\tilde{r}^{\prime 2}d\tilde{r}^{\prime}\\
+\int_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}\left(2\tilde{p}_{s}+\tilde{m}_{s}\frac{\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}^{2}}{\tilde{r}^{\prime 2}\tilde{n}_{s}}+\tilde{m}_{s}\tilde{n}_{s}\tilde{r}^{\prime 2}\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{2}\right)\tilde{r}^{\prime}d\tilde{r}^{\prime}\\
+\frac{\epsilon}{\tilde{\rho}_{p0}}\sum_{s^{\prime}}\int_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}\left(\tilde{m}_{s^{\prime}}\tilde{\nu}_{s^{\prime}s}\tilde{\Gamma}_{s^{\prime}}-\tilde{m}_{s}\tilde{\nu}_{ss^{\prime}}\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}\right)r^{\prime}dr^{\prime}\\
+\tilde{\rho}_{p0}\tilde{r}^{3}\left[\epsilon\tilde{\eta}_{s1}\frac{\partial}{\partial\tilde{r}}\left(\frac{\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}}{\tilde{r}^{2}\tilde{n}_{s}}\right)+\tilde{\eta}_{s3}\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{\prime}\right]_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}, $$

To leading order, $\mathcal{O}(\tilde{\rho}_{p0}^{-1})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{p}_{s}^{(-1,0)^{\prime}}=Z_{s}\tilde{n}_{s}\left(\tilde{E}_{r}^{(0,0)}+\tilde{r}\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{(0,0)}\tilde{B}_{z}\right), $$

where $\tilde{p}_{s}^{(-1,0)^{\prime}}$ is understood as resulting from temperature gradients that are of $\mathcal{O}(\tilde{\rho}_{p0}^{-1})$ . This is the case in the numerical example in section IV, when $\tilde{\rho}_{p0}=0.1$ .

Equation (61) is deceptive, as it seems to imply the leading order rotation is an $\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}$ drift. However, one arrives at this equation after solving for $\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{(0,0)}$ . This equation actually defines the electric field profile. This assertion is reflected in figures 3 and 4, in which the sum of the non-monotonous pressure gradient and electric field terms cancel each other such that the remainder is the monotonous angular velocity. In these figures this is the case for both $\tilde{\rho}_{p0}=0.1$ and $0.01$ .

To $\mathcal{O}(1)$ , subtracting equation (60) for $s=s^{\prime}$ from itself with $s=s$ ,

$$ \tilde{\omega}_{s^{\prime}}^{(1,0)}-\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{(1,0)}=\frac{\tilde{p}_{s^{\prime}}^{\prime(0,0)}}{Z_{s^{\prime}}\tilde{n}_{s^{\prime}}\tilde{r}\tilde{B}_{z}}-\frac{\tilde{m}_{s^{\prime}}\tilde{\omega}_{s^{\prime}}^{(0,0)^{2}}}{Z_{s^{\prime}}\tilde{B}_{z}}\\
-\frac{\tilde{p}_{s}^{\prime(0,0)}}{Z_{s}\tilde{n}_{s}\tilde{r}\tilde{B}_{z}}+\frac{\tilde{m}_{s}\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{(0,0)^{2}}}{Z_{s}\tilde{B}_{z}}, $$

allows us to achieve a non-ambiguous expression, to be substituted in equation (54).

The dimensionless equation (39),

$$ \sum_{s}\left[\tilde{m}_{s}\frac{\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}^{2}}{\tilde{n}_{s}}+\tilde{r}^{2}\tilde{p}_{s}\right]_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}=\frac{1}{\tilde{\rho}_{p0}}\sum_{s}Z_{s}\int_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}\tilde{n}_{s}\tilde{\omega}_{s}\tilde{B}_{z}\tilde{r}^{\prime 3}d\tilde{r}^{\prime}\\
+\sum_{s}\int_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}\left(2\tilde{p}_{s}+\tilde{m}_{s}\frac{\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}^{2}}{\tilde{r}^{\prime 2}\tilde{n}_{s}}+\tilde{m}_{s}\tilde{n}_{s}\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{2}\tilde{r}^{\prime 2}\right)\tilde{r}^{\prime}d\tilde{r}^{\prime}\\
+\tilde{\rho}_{p0}\sum_{s}\tilde{r}^{3}\left[\epsilon\tilde{\eta}_{s1}\frac{\partial}{\partial\tilde{r}}\left(\frac{\tilde{\Gamma}_{s}}{\tilde{r}^{2}\tilde{n}_{s}}\right)+\tilde{\eta}_{s3}\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{\prime}\right]_{\tilde{r}_{i}}^{\tilde{r}}. $$

To leading order, using Ampere’s law, this is an equation for the magnetic field,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{s}\tilde{p}_{s}^{\prime}+\tilde{r}\tilde{\omega}_{s}^{(0,0)^{2}}\sum_{s}\tilde{m}_{s}\tilde{n}_{s}=\mu_{0}^{-1}\frac{\partial\tilde{B}_{z}^{(1,0)}}{\partial\tilde{r}}\tilde{B}_{z}. $$

In this section we derived the leading and first order correction equations for the angular velocity profile, and the leading order equations for the density and magnetic field. We have shown how different particle flux magnitudes affect the solution, and suggested an interpretation of the relation between the leading order rotation and the electric field.

## VI Conclusion

The code MITNS: Multiple-Ion Transport Numerical Solver, was expanded to include a cylindrical coordinate mode, and used to validate the first-order solution to the rotation frequency and density distribution in a source-driven, axially magnetized, rotating two-fluid plasma cylinder presented in Kolmes et al. [30].

First, simulation results pointed to the error in the plotting script for Figure 3 in [30], and we were able to correct it in Figure 1.

Second, we have shown the approach to steady-state should be performed carefully, with appropriate magnetic boundary conditions, or else particle fluxes out of the simulation domain will deplete the magnetic field.

Third, after requiring a constant magnetic flux in the cylinder, the results of the MITNS code and the ODE set solution were shown to be congruent in the limit of small Larmor radius over domain size. This lends credibility to the MITNS code and its cylindrical coordinates mode.

Finally, we derived the rotation frequency, density and magnetic field equations, and suggested an interpretation to the relation between the electric field and rotation profile.

## Appendix A Using the particle source-term as a proxy for the axial dimension

In a steady state, azimuthally-symmetric cylinder and in the absence of particle source terms, the continuity equation can be written as,

$$ \displaystyle\nabla\cdot(n_{s}\mathbf{v}_{s})=\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(rn_{s}v_{sr})+\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(n_{s}v_{sz})=s_{s}^{\mathrm{source}}, $$

in the presence of fusion or ionization / recombination processes. $s_{s}^{\mathrm{source}}$ should be understood as a charge preserving in the sense $\sum_{s}Z_{s}s_{s}^{\mathrm{source}}=0$ .

We are interested in the result of radial variation, so we can treat the $\frac{\partial}{\partial z}$ part of the divergence as an additional source term,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(rn_{s}v_{sr})=s_{s}=s_{s}^{\mathrm{source}}-\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(n_{s}v_{sz}). $$

Identifying part of the source term with out-of-plane flow allows for charge / current source, where the electric charge weighted sum of electron and ion sources and sinks does not sum to zero.

Similarly for the momentum equation, we have a degree of freedom in $\mathbf{v}_{s}^{src}$ . Noticing the $\frac{\partial}{\partial z}$ component of $n_{s}\left(\mathbf{v}_{s}\cdot\nabla\right)\mathbf{v}_{s}$ is $n_{s}v_{z}\frac{\partial\mathbf{v}_{s}}{\partial z}$ , we can choose $\mathbf{v}_{s}^{src}$ such that:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{s}^{src}=\mathbf{v}+\frac{n_{s}v_{sz}}{\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(n_{s}v_{sz})-s_{s}^{\mathrm{source}}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{v}}{\partial z}=\mathbf{v}-\frac{n_{s}v_{sz}}{s_{s}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{v}}{\partial z} $$

Interpretation of the particle and velocity source terms as equations (66) and (67) allows us to solve for 2d ”slices” of a long cylindrical device. This is a method of getting an electric current source term that is large and entirely described by classical transport.

It is also possible to interpret the volumetric radial current source as being produced by a wave-particle interaction. In this picture, the wave is not modeled using the electromagnetic fields, due to its fast time-scales, and only pushes a current. Its ponderomotive force might appear as a momentum source term.

Another interpretation to the current source might be an externally-imposed shift in the magnetic field, which carries with it the electron fluid before friction is able to diffuse the field back.

## Appendix B Resolving radial current in a 1D Magneto-hydrodynamic multiple fluid simulation

The equations solved in MITNS, (1) and (2), are ”MHD-like”. Fast time-scales are discarded, such as the electric field term in Ampere’s law, in addition to the electron density and inertia terms.

Without the time derivatives in the electron continuity and momentum equations, the electron fluid density and velocity is evaluated algebraically from quasi-neutrality,

$$ \displaystyle n_{e}=\sum_{s\neq e}Z_{s}n_{s}, $$

and form Ampere’s law,

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{0}en_{e}\mathbf{v}_{e}=\mu_{0}\sum_{s\neq e}Z_{s}en_{s}\mathbf{v}_{s}-\nabla\times\mathbf{B}. $$

Quasi-neutrality makes Gauss Law inapplicable for a non-zero electric field. Instead, the electric field is determined from the inertia-less and non-viscous electron momentum equations. This electric field is also used to evolve the magnetic field.

MITNS has a one-dimensional domain, which restricts the allowed variations to the radial direction. If $\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}=\frac{\partial}{\partial z}=0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\nabla\times\mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{r}\equiv 0,~ $$

and no current can flow in the radial direction.

In order to explore radial plasma conductivity in this framework, that is, to look at the relation between $j_{r}$ and the other physical quantities in the system, we must ignore equation (70), and instead implement a current on the entire domain, similarly to a body force (such as gravity),

$$ \displaystyle v_{er}=\left[\sum_{s\neq e}Z_{s}n_{s}\right]^{-1}\cdot\left[\sum_{s\neq e}Z_{s}n_{s}v_{sr}-j_{r}(r,t)\right]. $$

The function $j_{r}(r,t)$ has to be specified either as a local Ohm’s law, or as an a-priori driving force.

The algebraic nature of the ”MHD-like” electric field prevents an application of boundary conditions to the electron momentum equation or to the electric field.

Azimuthal current can be injected into the simulated domain by applying a boundary condition to the magnetic field.

This solution adds to the electron velocity perpendicularly to the magnetic field. This does not represents a cross-field transport of the electrons, as the magnetic field would be advected by the moving electron fluid. Adding the current to the electrons is numerically simple, and its effects are automatically implemented in the friction terms and magnetic field evolution. It also avoids changing the accurate ion momentum equations. Attempting to add the imposed current to the ion velocities would require some partition of the current among an arbitrary number of ion fluids.

It is possible to evaluate, in post processing, the departure from quasi-neutrality using Gauss law by taking the divergence of the electric field calculated using Ohm’s law. The current relates to the displacement current by,

$$ \displaystyle\nabla\cdot\mathbf{j}=-\varepsilon_{0}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}, \displaystyle j_{r}=\frac{r_{i}j_{r}(r_{i})}{r}-\varepsilon_{0}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(E_{r}-\frac{r_{i}E_{r}(r_{i})}{r}\right), $$

which would be a small, of $\mathcal{O}(v_{A}^{2}/c^{2})$ , with $v_{A}$ being the Alfvén speed, and $c$ the speed of light.
